## Named Continuous Distributions

In this tutorial, you will work with:

-   Continuous Uniform distribution
-   Normal distribution

You should be able to:

-   Identify the distribution\
-   Compute probabilities using R\
-   Use density, cumulative distribution, quantile, and simulation functions\
-   Interpret results correctly

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Part 1: Continuous Uniform Distribution

### Bus Waiting Time Example

A bus arrives every 10 minutes. A student arrives at a random time.

Let:

X \~ Unif(0,10)

-   pdf: f(x) = 1/10 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 10\
-   All waiting times between 0 and 10 are equally likely.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Probability 1: Waiting time 5 minutes or less

Compute: $P(X \leq 5)$

```{r unif1, exercise=TRUE,  exercise.eval=FALSE} 
# Use punif()
```

```{r unif1-solution} 
punif(5, min = 0, max = 10)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Probability 2: Waiting time between 5 and 7 minutes

Compute: $P(5 \leq X \leq 7)$

```{r unif2, exercise=TRUE,  exercise.eval=FALSE}
# Use difference of two CDF values
```

```{r unif2-solution} 
punif(7, min = 0, max = 10) -    punif(5, min = 0, max = 10)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Probability 3: Waiting time more than 6 minutes

Compute: $P(X \geq 6)$

```{r unif3, exercise=TRUE, exercise.eval=FALSE} 
# Use lower.tail = FALSE
```

```{r unif3-solution} 
punif(6, min = 0, max = 10, lower.tail = FALSE)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Uniform Distribution Functions in R

For X \~ Unif(a,b):

-   dunif(x, min, max) → density\
-   punif(q, min, max) → cumulative probability\
-   qunif(p, min, max) → quantile\
-   runif(n, min, max) → random sample

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Generate 5 observations from Unif(0,10)

```{r unif4, exercise=TRUE, exercise.eval=FALSE} 
# Generate 5 values
```

```{r unif4-solution} 
runif(5, min = 0, max = 10)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Generate 1000 observations and visualize

```{r unif5, exercise=TRUE, exercise.eval=FALSE} 
# Generate and plot
```

```{r unif5-solution} 
x <- runif(1000, min = 0, max = 10) 
hist(x, breaks = 20, probability = TRUE) 
abline(h = 1/10, lwd = 2)
```

Notice the approximately flat shape --- all values are equally likely.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Part 2: Normal Distribution

### Key Properties

If:

$X \sim N(\mu,\sigma)$

-   Bell-shaped\
-   Symmetric about μ\
-   Mean = Median = Mode\
-   Total area under curve = 1\
-   Determined by mean ($\mu$) and standard deviation ($\sigma$)

Standard normal: $Z \sim N(0,1)$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Normal Distribution Functions in R

For $X \sim N(\mu,\sigma)$:

-   dnorm(x, mean, sd) → density\
-   pnorm(q, mean, sd) → cumulative probability\
-   qnorm(p, mean, sd) → quantile\
-   rnorm(n, mean, sd) → random sample

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Plot the Standard Normal Density

```{r normal1, exercise=TRUE, exercise.eval=FALSE} 
# Plot N(0,1)
```

```{r normal1-solution} 
x <- seq(-3, 3, by = 0.01) 
y <- dnorm(x) 
plot(x, y, type = "l", lwd = 2,      
     main = "Standard Normal Density",      
     xlab = "x", ylab = "Density")
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Probability: P(X ≤ 2) where X \~ N(1,1.5)

```{r normal2, exercise=TRUE, exercise.eval=FALSE} 
# Use pnorm()
```

```{r normal2-solution, exercise.eval=FALSE} 
pnorm(2, mean = 1, sd = 1.5)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Probability: P(X \> 2)

```{r normal3, exercise=TRUE, exercise.eval=FALSE} 
# Use lower.tail = FALSE
```

```{r normal3-solution} 
pnorm(2, mean = 1, sd = 1.5, lower.tail = FALSE)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Probability: P(0 ≤ X ≤ 2)

```{r normal4, exercise=TRUE, exercise.eval=FALSE} 
# Difference of two CDFs
```

```{r normal4-solution} 
pnorm(2, mean = 1, sd = 1.5) -   pnorm(0, mean = 1, sd = 1.5)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Find the 90th percentile of N(1,1.5)

```{r normal5, exercise=TRUE, exercise.eval=FALSE} 
# Use qnorm()
```

```{r normal5-solution} 
qnorm(0.90, mean = 1, sd = 1.5)
```

Interpretation: 90% of observations fall below this value.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Simulate 1000 observations and visualize

```{r normal6, exercise=TRUE, exercise.eval=FALSE} 
# Simulate and plot
```

```{r normal6-solution} 
set.seed(123) 
x <- rnorm(1000, mean = 1, sd = 1.5) 
hist(x, breaks = 30, probability = TRUE) 
curve(dnorm(x, mean = 1, sd = 1.5), add = TRUE, lwd = 2)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Check the 68% Rule for Standard Normal

Compute:

P(-1 ≤ Z ≤ 1)

```{r normal7, exercise=TRUE, exercise.eval=FALSE} 
# Your code here
```

```{r normal7-solution} 
pnorm(1) - pnorm(-1)
```

You should obtain approximately 0.68.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Summary

For continuous distributions:

-   Probability = Area under the curve\
-   d → density\
-   p → cumulative probability\
-   q → quantile\
-   r → simulation

You should now be able to:

-   Identify Uniform vs Normal\
-   Compute probabilities correctly\
-   Find percentiles\
-   Simulate observations\
-   Interpret results in context
